source.title: Cross-Domain Graph Data Scaling: A Showcase with Diffusion Models
source.authors: Wenzhuo Tang; Hai-Tao Mao; Danial Dervovic; Ivan Brugere; Saumitra Mishra; Yuying Xie; Ji-Liang Tang

record.tranche_reason: Applies the general data/compute scaling idea to graph diffusion models and reports downstream results in that new setting. It does not measure the language-model loss laws or fit power laws.
record.gate_note: The paper cites neural scaling laws and investigates graph-data scale and pre-training compute. Its outcomes are downstream graph-task metrics, not held-out cross-entropy loss or fitted power laws. Those outcomes are recorded as findings about scaling in graphs, not as evidence for the versions that specifically require power-law loss behavior. Other benchmark comparisons are omitted because they do not bear on the scaling results.
record.test_reason: The paper cites neural scaling laws as motivation and runs graph-specific scaling experiments. These cover three pre-training collections (SMALL/FULL/EXTRA), 25–100% stratified subsets, and five checkpoints of one run spanning 5–25×10^-3 PF-days. Every outcome is a downstream graph-task metric (accuracy, MRR, Hits@10) for a graph diffusion augmentor. No held-out loss is reported, no power law is fitted or extrapolated, model size is never varied, and there is no compute-optimal allocation or shape comparison. The results show only that more data or compute generally helps, over less than one order of magnitude of compute. That is a related but different construct from any version's power-law or predictability claim, so it is recorded under fits_no_version rather than as a test. V5 would require the power-law form in a new modality. V6 concerns predictable downstream gains for language models with scale or loss; here no predictive relation is fitted, the series are non-monotonic, and the model is not a language model.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that UniAug gives consistent gains across node-, link- and graph-level tasks. They also say downstream performance improves with pre-training data scale and diversity: SMALL/FULL/EXTRA plus the 25–75% subsets point to both quantity and diversity mattering. Performance improves with compute, with slowing on some datasets. They do not study model size, owing to limited resources, and only anticipate that larger models would help.
record.recipe_differences: A graph-structure diffusion and downstream augmentation study, not a reproduction of language-model scaling-law methods; it reports qualitative downstream performance trends rather than fitted loss laws.
record.method_sensitivity: Data collection and downstream dataset change the reported performance; some data-scale and compute sequences are non-monotonic.

fits_no_version.finding: Downstream graph-classification and link-prediction metrics mostly rise from SMALL to FULL to EXTRA pre-training collections, with exceptions. Enzymes FULL 71.33 vs EXTRA 71.17; Erdos FULL 36.07 below SMALL 36.28; SMALL falls below the non-pretrained baseline on IMDB-B, IMDB-M and Citeseer.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Graph diffusion augmentors benefit downstream from larger and more diverse cross-domain pre-training graph collections.

fits_no_version.finding: Across checkpoints of one training run (5–25×10^-3 PF-days), downstream metrics generally rise but fluctuate. Examples: Enzymes and IMDB-B dip at 15, Citeseer dips at 15, Proteins dips at 20. Authors say gains slow for some datasets near 8,000 epochs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Longer pre-training of a graph diffusion augmentor generally improves downstream graph-task performance, with dataset-dependent plateaus.

record.code_released: Code stated to be in the supplemental material; URL not stated.
record.peer_reviewed: NeurIPS 2025 (39th Conference, as stated in the text)
record.problems: The study does not fit or evaluate power laws and reports neither language-model loss nor parameter/token scaling. The graph scaling evidence uses downstream task metrics, and some series are non-monotonic; the authors also note they did not investigate model-parameter effects due to limited resources.
record.rows_left_out: Kept all 27 data-collection comparisons and all 20 graph-classification compute checkpoints. To stay within 60 rows, retained compute checkpoints for Cora and Citeseer and the first three Power checkpoints; omitted Power at 20 and 25 × 10−3 PF-days and all compute checkpoints for Yeast and Erdos from Appendix D.4, Table 23. Other benchmark tables were outside the scaling results.

untested.parts: No language-model loss and no power-law fit in parameters, tokens or compute.
No fit on small runs and no extrapolation to larger runs.
No fixed-budget parameter/token allocation; model size is never varied (authors cite limited resources).
No depth/width comparison at fixed parameter count.
Graph-domain scaling is examined, but whether a power-law form holds is not tested; compute spans only 5x, data has three qualitative levels.
Downstream graph metrics rise loosely with data and compute, but no predictive fit and no relation to pretraining loss; not language models.
No exponents or fitting choices compared.

missing.what: Data-quantity-only scaling: stratified 25%, 50%, 75%, 100% subsets of the pre-training set, evaluated on 7 datasets. Authors report a clear upward trend; values are shown only in a figure. Not recorded and not declared in rows_left_out.

record.verdict_notes: Reader's 'tests/T3' is overridden: all reader version statuses were not_tested and no labels were given, which is inconsistent with 'tests'. Relation set to discusses/T6, with the graph scaling results kept as fits_no_version. The compute axis is checkpoints of a single run, not separate compute-matched runs, so it cannot speak to compute-optimal scaling. Row links (none) and states (cannot_determine) are appropriate.

versions.untested_parts: No language-model loss or loss scaling with parameter count, tokens, or compute is measured.
No small-run power-law fits or predictions for larger runs are reported.
No fixed-compute parameter/token allocation or compute-optimal split is studied.
No architecture-shape comparison at fixed parameter count is reported.
The study examines graph-task performance as graph pre-training data and compute increase, but does not test whether the same power-law form holds.
Downstream graph metrics are reported, but no language-model downstream performance or relationship to pretraining loss is measured.
No fitted exponents, fitting-method comparisons, or departures from a single power law are examined.
